I've been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when they rolled out the T-Mobile ONE plan. I enjoyed a military discount throughout, but even with that, combined with T-Mobile's price hikes, my monthly bill had crept up to $113. I'd had enough and started looking for something cheaper. On top of that, this year's iPhone 18 Pro costs at least $100 more, so saving money on my phone bill could help offset the cost of upgrading. That's why I started researching MVNOs.

What is an MVNO?

MVNO stands for "Mobile Virtual Network Operator." Simply put, an MVNO is a wireless service provider that doesn't own its own nationwide cellular network. Instead of building their own network, they buy capacity from major carriers like AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon and resell it to their own customers. Think of them as middlemen for wireless service.

Choosing an MVNO doesn't necessarily mean giving up the network you currently use. Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile's network, Visible uses Verizon's, and US Mobile lets customers choose between all three major networks. This article focuses on those three MVNOs, as they're the ones I researched most thoroughly before leaving T-Mobile, but there are many other options on the market.

At the end of the day, an MVNO is just another way to buy cellular service without going directly through a network operator.

Why are MVNOs cheaper? Are there any downsides?

If an MVNO is using the exact same network as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how can they charge so much less? The simple answer is that MVNOs don't have to shoulder all the costs of running a nationwide wireless carrier. They don't have to build or maintain networks, many operate primarily online rather than maintaining physical stores, and they have fewer employees. The money they save is passed on to customers in the form of lower monthly bills.

MVNO plans tend to be simpler, without the "perks" and extras that big carriers offer. Depending on the carrier and plan, you might not get free streaming services or other benefits that kept you with a major carrier. But if you really want those "free" things, the money you save with an MVNO is often enough to subscribe to those services yourself.

This is exactly my situation. I used to love the free MLB.TV subscription T-Mobile offered and used it every season, but I never watch Netflix, so "free Netflix" offers are completely useless to me. And even if I wanted Netflix plus MLB.TV, I could just subscribe to them myself and still come out ahead by switching. For me, the most important thing is having reliable, affordable cellular service—I don't need the extras T-Mobile provides.

The "downside" isn't necessarily that the service is worse, but that you're paying less and getting less. Exactly what you have to give up depends on which MVNO and plan you choose. Video streaming may be limited to lower resolution, high-speed or priority data allowances may differ, and network priority may be different. I have fast Wi-Fi at home and rarely go to places like concerts or sporting events where crowds can clog networks, so network priority doesn't impact my daily use much. But I do travel internationally occasionally, so international data is an important consideration for me. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, while others charge extra or have limited coverage.

There are also some less obvious differences, especially if you want to buy a new iPhone. If you go with an MVNO as your carrier, you can't use Apple Card installment payments or the iPhone Upgrade Program. Those options are limited to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. Practically speaking, if you buy your iPhone directly from Apple, you usually have to pay for it all at once. Big carriers can also offer large trade-in credits and promotions that MVNOs generally don't match. Not every MVNO supports Apple Watch, so if you use the cellular model, you'll want to check.

Finally, most MVNOs primarily offer support over the phone and online rather than having staff at stores to help you face-to-face. I consider myself fairly tech-savvy and didn't want to have to go to a store for minor issues. And based on my experience, store salespeople end up calling the same support line anyway, with the same wait times, so this doesn't deter me at all.

The key point is that none of these limitations apply to every MVNO—it all depends on the carrier and plan—so before you switch, be sure you understand exactly what you're getting.

Three MVNOs worth considering

After deciding to leave T-Mobile, I started looking at other options. Verizon and AT&T's postpaid plans were even more expensive than what I was already paying, so the other two major carriers were out. I ultimately narrowed my search down to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each had something different that appealed to me, and all three could help me significantly lower my monthly bill without sacrificing access to a major carrier's network.

US Mobile is arguably the most flexible of the three, and it's the carrier I ultimately moved to from T-Mobile. That doesn't mean it's the best fit for you, or even the best of the three. It's just the one that best matched my personal needs.

US Mobile wasn't my first choice—I had never even heard of the company before I started researching MVNOs. But the more I looked, the more it stood out. Here's why: US Mobile works on all three major networks in the US, letting customers choose the one that works best for them. It also offers a Multi-Network add-on that lets you activate two networks on the same iPhone (the add-on network's line runs in the background), so when your primary network's signal is weak or has no coverage, your iPhone can automatically switch to the other network (US Mobile calls this "when coverage is lower"). You need to enable "Allow Cellular Data Switching" in your iPhone's Cellular settings to use this feature. US Mobile charges extra for this add-on, and I personally didn't need it, but it's nice that the option exists.

I had just moved and wanted to see how Verizon's coverage compared to T-Mobile's near my new home, so I decided to try both. I put my wife's iPhone on US Mobile's Light Speed network (which is T-Mobile) and my own iPhone on Warp (which is Verizon) so I could compare coverage directly. In our area, Verizon was clearly better, so switching to US Mobile was a win-win: much lower monthly cost and even better coverage.

Mint Mobile was actually my first choice, because it's a T-Mobile sub-brand, meaning I'd be using the network I was already familiar with, but for much less. What I didn't like was that it didn't include international data. My wife and I love taking cruises and travel abroad frequently, so having cellular data while traveling is important to us. Mint does offer international data, but it's an extra charge that quickly eats into some of the savings. I also wasn't fond of the fact that taxes and fees are charged separately.

Visible is also pretty straightforward, but it only uses Verizon's network. My biggest concern with Visible was Verizon's coverage in my area. After nearly ten years with T-Mobile, I knew how its network performed, but I had no idea about Verizon's coverage. That alone made me initially choose US Mobile over Visible, because US Mobile let me try Verizon while still having the option to fall back to T-Mobile or AT&T if Verizon didn't work out. Visible's top unlimited data plan includes free cellular Apple Watch service, which is appealing. (US Mobile's Warp/Verizon network offers the same perk in its top plan.)

What you'll need to switch

Switching to an MVNO was easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones, and moving our two lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile took about 10 minutes. I never had to leave the couch. You'll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, though I'm focusing on iPhone), plus some information from your current carrier. If you want to keep your existing phone number, be sure not to cancel your current service until the number has been fully ported over.

You'll need the following:

  • Your current carrier's account number
  • Your port-out PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

I prepaid US Mobile for a full year of two unlimited data plans to prepare for the switch. My wife doesn't use a cellular Apple Watch and doesn't care about higher-quality video, so she chose US Mobile's Unlimited Starter plan, saving $100 over the Unlimited Premium plan I chose. Two lines plus an Apple Watch plan came to $500 a year, compared to the $1,356 a year my wife and I were paying T-Mobile for two lines without Apple Watch service. (Keep in mind, that price already includes my military discount.)

Getting the port-out PIN from T-Mobile was straightforward. I had expected this step to be hidden and complicated, but it wasn't. The steps for Verizon and AT&T are also listed below.

Once my iPhone was connected to Wi-Fi, US Mobile sent over a new eSIM, and the installation process was as simple as clicking a button in an email and following a few prompts. My wife's iPhone followed the same steps. The only additional step was setting up my Apple Watch, which I did easily through the US Mobile app.

Why I'll continue using an MVNO

Same coverage, lower bill: When I calculate how much I'm saving, the trade-offs I've made are absolutely worth it. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, so I don't burn through much cellular data (though based on speed tests, US Mobile is just as fast as T-Mobile). Most importantly, when I'm not on Wi-Fi, my cellular signal is still strong and stable, especially for calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have actually done away with traditional contracts in favor of device installment plans, which are essentially just another way to lock you into their network until you've paid off the device. I've always bought my iPhones directly from Apple because I value the freedom of having an unlocked phone, but I also appreciate that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible all don't require contracts.

Switching is easy: Most MVNOs let you pay month to month, so you're not locked into a long-term contract. If one carrier has a great promotion this month and another has an even better deal next month, you can switch quickly and easily. Prepaid accounts also don't require a credit check—which means when you switch, you won't have a hard inquiry on your credit report dragging down your credit score the way you would with a postpaid account, and you won't be denied because of your credit history. My credit is fine, but even switching from T-Mobile to Verizon, I wouldn't want a hard inquiry on my record.

Top comment from Richard Lewis (Rich),

A few years ago I left AT&T for Mint Mobile. It's one of the smartest tech decisions I've made.

Save more by paying annually: The trade-off for flexibility is that if you're willing to prepay for a full year of service upfront, you can save even more. Most MVNOs offer significant discounts on annual plans, so you're balancing the freedom to switch anytime against a lower overall cost.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I love taking cruises. If you've ever boarded a ship and forgotten to turn on airplane mode, only to have your iPhone automatically connect to the ship's network, you know how painful the bill can be. With a prepaid plan, you don't have to worry about accidentally racking up a massive roaming bill. Unless international roaming is included, my phone simply won't connect to a foreign network and charge me. US Mobile's plans also include taxes and fees, so what you see is what you pay.

Switching to an MVNO isn't about chasing the absolute cheapest service—it's about paying a reasonable price for exactly what you need, rather than paying for a bunch of stuff you don't need. So far, I don't feel like I've missed out on anything that matters to me (though I know I'll miss that free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I've gained a cellular Apple Watch line I didn't have before, all for a lower monthly cost. My iPhone hasn't changed, my phone number hasn't changed, the coverage I'm getting on US Mobile's Warp (Verizon) network is even better than before—and I still have the freedom to switch again whenever I want.

Your priorities may be different from mine, and MVNOs aren't for everyone. But if you're currently paying a lot for cellular service and haven't considered an MVNO, it's worth a look. You may be surprised at how little you actually have to give up.
